screens.title: What is an EC2 instance?
screens.narratorSegment: An EC2 instance is simply a virtual machine running on AWS infrastructure that provides compute capacity for your application. Think of it as a server you control: you decide the operating system, installed software, and lifecycle. The elastic part of EC2 means instances can be launched or terminated quickly so compute scales with demand; you pay for the capacity you use while it runs. A concrete example is creating an EC2 instance to host a small web application: you select an AMI with the desired operating system, pick an instance type like t2. micro for low traffic, and attach an EBS volume to persist site content. Common misconceptions include assuming an instance automatically backs up data when stopped; EBS volumes remain separate and snapshots are required for backups. Also remember that instance runtime cost stops when you terminate the instance, but attached EBS volumes may still incur charges. The key takeaway is that EC2 gives you precise control over server configuration coupled with the ability to scale and pay only for what you use. When you plan an architecture, ask whether a long-running instance or a more scalable service is the best fit for the workload.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is an EC2 instance?

EC2 instance — term and meaning

A virtual server that runs on AWS hardware, configurable with an AMI, instance type, and attached storage.

Example
Host a static website on Amazon Linux using t2.micro for testing.
Misconception
Stopping an instance is not a backup; create EBS snapshots for durability.
Why elasticity matters
  • Scale capacity up or down to match demand and control cost.
  • Launch instances quickly from AMIs to create consistent environments.
  • Choose instance types to balance performance and price for the workload.
Key Takeaway

Treat an EC2 instance as a controllable, ephemeral server; pair it with EBS snapshots for persistence and choose instance types to match workload needs.

Quick facts

AMI: template to start instance

Key pair: SSH cryptographic key for access

Security Group: virtual firewall rules

EBS: persistent block storage

screens.title: AMIs: Amazon Machine Images
screens.narratorSegment: An Amazon Machine Image, or AMI, is the template used to launch an EC2 instance. It contains the operating system and any software you want installed at launch. AWS supplies official AMIs for Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, and Windows Server, and you can create custom AMIs from a configured instance to standardize deployments. A common example is building a custom AMI that includes your application server and dependencies, then launching many instances from that AMI to ensure identical runtime behavior. One pitfall is relying on a public AMI without verifying its contents; create or use vetted AMIs for production. Creating your own AMI helps speed scaling and reduces configuration drift because each launch begins from the same snapshot. Remember that AMIs are region-specific; if you operate across regions, copy AMIs as part of your deployment pipeline. The practical effect is reproducible servers and faster scale-out. Consider AMIs part of your release artifact: they capture a known-good state that can be re-launched reliably when you need more compute. AMIs: Amazon Machine Images means amis package os and software so instances launch consistently; custom amis reduce configuration drift and accelerate scaling.. In practical terms, templates that define an instance's software configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › AMIs: Amazon Machine Images

What an AMI contains and why it matters

An AMI is the immutable template for your instance's OS and preinstalled software, used to ensure consistent launches.

Use case
Create an AMI that bundles your web server and common libraries so you can scale identical servers quickly.
Practical note
AMIs are region-specific. Copy them when deploying to other regions to preserve consistency.
Misconception
Do not assume a public AMI is secure; verify contents before using in production.
Key Takeaway

Treat AMIs as release artifacts: build, verify, and reuse them to ensure identical environments across launches.

AMI examples
  • Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Red Hat supplied by AWS
  • Custom AMI copied from a configured instance
  • Use AMIs for automated scale-out and consistent deployments
Next: instance types and how they match workload needs.

screens.title: EC2 Instance Types
screens.narratorSegment: Instance types define the hardware profile for an EC2 instance: C P U, memory, storage capacity, and networking. AWS groups types into families with clear primary uses. General purpose (M series) balances resources for mixed workloads. Compute optimized (C series) favors C P U-heavy tasks like batch compute or high-performance web servers. Memory optimized (R series) suits in-memory databases or analytics, while storage optimized (I series) is for high IOPS disk workloads. Accelerated computing (P/G series) provides GPUs for machine learning or graphics acceleration. A concrete example: choose an R series instance for an in-memory cache or a large in-memory database because it provides high R A M relative to C P U. A common planning error is selecting an instance type based only on C P U numbers without considering memory-to-C P U ratio or network bandwidth; this can cause performance bottlenecks. Right-sizing means profiling your workload and selecting an instance that meets both performance and cost goals. If cost is primary and the workload is fault tolerant, consider a lower-cost family or Spot Instances, but be aware of interruption risk. Matching instance family to workload characteristics is essential for predictable performance and efficient spend.

keyIdea.text: Pick instance families by workload: M for balance, C for CPU, R for memory, I for storage, P/G for acceleration.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › EC2 Instance Types

Choose by primary workload need

Instance types focus resources where a workload needs them most; pick based on CPU, memory, storage I/O, or acceleration.

General purpose — M
Balanced CPU and memory for general applications.
Compute optimized — C
High CPU for compute-bound tasks and batch processing.
Memory optimized — R
Large memory footprint for caches and in-memory DBs.
Storage optimized — I
High IOPS and throughput for disk-heavy workloads.
Accelerated — P/G
GPU-based instances for ML or graphics acceleration.
Key Takeaway

Match an instance type to the dominant resource need of your workload to avoid throughput or latency bottlenecks.

Right-sizing tips
  • Profile CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network before choosing.
  • Avoid choosing on core count alone; check memory and bandwidth.
  • Consider testing multiple families under real load.
Next: cost models and purchasing options.

screens.title: EC2 Purchasing Options
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 purchasing options change the cost and availability trade-offs of your compute. On-Demand lets you pay for capacity by the hour or second with no long-term commitments, ideal for unpredictable or short-lived workloads. Reserved Instances provide significant discounts in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment and suit steady-state workloads where usage is predictable. Savings Plans extend this concept, offering discounts across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda in return for a commitment to a consistent hourly spend, which gives more flexibility than instance-specific reservations. Spot Instances let you use unused capacity at deep discounts for fault-tolerant workloads that can accept interruptions. A concrete scenario: for a nightly batch job that can resume work, Spot Instances may be cost-optimal, while a production database benefits from Reserved pricing for consistency. A common mistake is overcommitting to reservations without measuring steady-state usage, which wastes cost savings if utilization is low. The recommended approach is to measure baseline usage, use Reserved or Savings Plans for the predictable portion, and supplement with On-Demand or Spot for bursts or flexible tasks. That balance achieves cost efficiency without sacrificing required availability.

keyIdea.text: Use On-Demand for flexibility, Reserved/Savings for steady workloads, and Spot for interruptible, cost-sensitive tasks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › EC2 Purchasing Options

Selecting a pricing model

Each option affects your cost profile and suitability for different workloads.

On-Demand
Pay-as-you-go for short-lived or unpredictable workloads with no commitment.
Reserved Instances
Discounts for 1- or 3-year commitments; best for steady usage.
Savings Plans
More flexible commitment measured by hourly spend across services.
Spot Instances
Low-cost compute for fault-tolerant workloads that can tolerate interruptions.
Scenario

For nightly batch analytics that restarts on failure, use Spot for cost savings. For a critical database, use Reserved or Savings Plans for predictable pricing.

Decision guide
  1. Measure baseline usage.
  2. Commit for predictable portion (RI or Savings).
  3. Use Spot or On-Demand for variable or interruptible parts.
Avoid overcommitting before you understand steady-state usage.

screens.title: Key Pairs and SSH Access
screens.narratorSegment: Key pairs secure SSH access to Linux EC2 instances. A key pair includes a public key, which AWS stores, and a private key file you download and keep locally. When you launch a Linux instance, you assign a key pair so you can SSH into the instance using the private key. Keep the private key file secure; for example, use file permissions that restrict access to your user account. The chapter's hands-on example creates a key pair named my-web-server-key and downloads my-web-server-key. pem. A common mistake is storing the private key in an unsafe location or sharing it. Another misstep is not setting file permissions correctly; SSH clients will refuse to use an insecure key file. For Windows instances, key pairs let you decrypt the administrator password. Practically, treat the private key like a secret credential. If it is lost or compromised, create a new key pair and update access procedures. For automated deployments, use secure secret management and avoid embedding private keys in scripts. Remember: key pairs control direct host access and are a crucial first line of defense for instances.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Key Pairs and SSH Access

How key pairs work

Key pairs use public-key cryptography to prove identity when establishing SSH sessions to Linux instances.

Create and protect
Create a key pair when launching an instance and download the .pem file. Restrict file permissions to keep the private key safe.
Common error
Do not allow broad read access to your private key; SSH clients may refuse to use insecure files.
Windows instances
Key pairs decrypt the administrator password for Windows servers; protect the key like any secret.
Key Takeaway

Treat private keys as secrets. Protect them with strict permissions and rotate keys or replace them if compromised.

Practical checklist
  • Create a new key pair for production servers.
  • Download the .pem file and set chmod 400 on Unix systems.
  • Use secure secret storage for automated credentials.
Next: Security Groups and firewall rules.

screens.title: Security Groups: virtual firewalls
screens.narratorSegment: Security Groups are stateful virtual firewalls that control network traffic to and from EC2 instances. They define allowed inbound and outbound rules by protocol, port range, and source or destination IP ranges. For example, to allow SSH access, add an inbound rule for TCP port 22 from your IP address; to serve a website, allow inbound HTTP on port 80 from anywhere if public access is needed. A frequent security flaw is making rules too permissive, such as allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0, which exposes instances to wide attack surface. Follow the principle of least privilege: open only the ports you need, and restrict the source IP ranges to trusted addresses whenever possible. Security Groups are applied at the instance level, and changes apply immediately to associated instances. Because they are stateful, an allowed inbound connection will automatically allow return traffic; you usually don't need explicit outbound rules for the same connection. Always review Security Group rules during deployment to ensure they match intended access patterns. Security Groups: virtual firewalls means security groups are stateful firewalls; use least privilege and avoid open ssh access from everywhere.. In practical terms, control inbound and outbound traffic using allowed protocols, ports, and sources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Security Groups: virtual firewalls

How Security Groups protect instances

Define allowed inbound and outbound traffic with rules that include protocol, port, and source/destination ranges.

Example rules
SSH: TCP 22 from My IP. HTTP: TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 if public web access is required.
Common mistake
Allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 opens access to the entire internet and increases risk. Restrict to known IPs.
Stateful behavior
Security Groups are stateful: return traffic is automatically allowed for established connections.
Action

Always restrict inbound rules to the smallest required source range and document why each port is open.

Checklist
  • Use specific IP ranges for SSH access.
  • Allow only necessary ports for each role.
  • Review and tighten rules as deployments evolve.
Next: EBS volumes and types.

screens.title: EBS Volumes: persistent block storage
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Elastic Block Store provides persistent block-level storage that you attach to EC2 instances. EBS volumes persist independently from the instance’s lifetime, so your data can survive instance termination when configured to do so. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › EBS Volumes: persistent block storage

EBS volume types and when to use them

Pick EBS volume types by throughput, IOPS, and cost profile to match your application’s storage needs.

General Purpose SSD — gp2 / gp3
Balanced performance for most applications.
Provisioned IOPS SSD — io1 / io2
High, consistent IOPS for databases and latency-sensitive workloads.
Throughput Optimized HDD — st1
High throughput for big data and large sequential I/O.
Cold HDD — sc1
Lowest cost for infrequent access workloads.
Key Takeaway

Choose EBS based on IO and throughput needs, then protect data with snapshot backups to meet recovery objectives.

Practical tips
  • Use gp3 for typical app disks.
  • Use io2 for production databases needing sustained IOPS.
  • Use snapshots regularly to protect data.
Next: snapshots and lifecycle management.

screens.title: EBS Snapshots and Backup Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: EBS snapshots are incremental backups of EBS volumes stored in object storage, enabling point-in-time recovery and migration. Snapshots save only changed blocks after the initial snapshot, helping to reduce storage costs over time. To ensure durability, schedule regular snapshots based on your recovery point objective and test restores to verify the process. For example, daily snapshots might be appropriate for production databases while weekly snapshots could suffice for less critical data. A frequent oversight is assuming snapshots are instantaneous; depending on volume size and input and output load, snapshots may take time to complete. Another common error is not automating cleanup policies, which can lead to unexpected costs from old snapshots. Implement lifecycle policies that remove or archive snapshots according to retention rules. When restoring, you create a new EBS volume from a snapshot and attach it to an instance. In migration scenarios, snapshots let you copy data across regions by copying the snapshot to the target region and restoring a volume there. Always test your snapshot and restore process to confirm you meet your recovery objectives. EBS Snapshots and Backup Strategy means use incremental ebs snapshots with retention and lifecycle policies; test restores to ensure recoverability.. In practical terms, create incremental backups and plan for recovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Snapshots and lifecycle

Snapshots are incremental backups stored outside the instance lifecycle. They let you restore volumes or move data between regions.

Incremental behavior
After the first full snapshot, only changed blocks are saved on subsequent snapshots, saving space and time.
Best practice
Automate snapshot schedules and retention policies to balance cost and recovery needs.
Restore workflow
Create a new EBS volume from a snapshot and attach it to an instance to recover data.
Key Takeaway

Schedule incremental snapshots, apply lifecycle retention, and test restores to make backups reliable and cost-effective.

Snapshot checklist
  • Automate snapshot creation.
  • Define retention and cleanup policies.
  • Test restores regularly.

screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through launching a secure web server on EC2 using the console choices described in the chapter. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Connect and Install Nginx — Terminal Commands

Command sequence

Use these terminal commands to securely connect and install Nginx on Amazon Linux.

chmod 400 my-web-server-key.pem
ssh -i "my-web-server-key.pem" ec2-user@YOUR_INSTANCE_PUBLIC_IP

sudo yum update -y
sudo yum install nginx -y
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx
Check

If Nginx is running, visit the instance public IP in a browser to see the welcome page. If not, confirm Security Group allows HTTP.

Notes
  • Replace YOUR_INSTANCE_PUBLIC_IP with the value from the console.
  • Use chmod to restrict key file permissions.
  • Open HTTP in Security Group to view the page publicly.
Remember: never share your private key file. Rotate keys if exposed.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: This screen highlights common mistakes and how to avoid them when working with EC2. One frequent error is overly permissive Security Groups—allowing SSH from everywhere is risky. Use your specific IP address or a narrow range for SSH. Another mistake is selecting an instance type based only on C P U without considering memory or network bandwidth, which can create bottlenecks. When it comes to storage, choosing a low-cost HDD for a latency-sensitive database will harm performance; select gp3 or io2 according to IOPS and throughput needs. For purchasing options, avoid committing to Reserved Instances before measuring steady-state usage; instead collect usage data and then commit to RIs or Savings Plans for the predictable portion. With key pairs, the common operational issue is losing the private key or storing it in an insecure location; treat it as a secret and rotate when necessary. For snapshots, failing to automate retention leads to uncontrolled costs. The best practices are clear: apply least privilege, right-size based on profiling, automate backups and lifecycle, and test restores. These patterns reduce risk and keep cost predictable.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Common Mistakes and Best Practices

Avoid these pitfalls

Practical checks to prevent security, performance, and cost issues.

Security: SSH exposure
Do not allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. Restrict to known IP ranges and use least privilege.
Sizing: CPU vs memory
Profile your workload. Don't choose an instance by CPU alone; check memory and network bandwidth.
Storage: wrong volume
Match EBS type to access pattern: gp3 for balanced, io2 for high IOPS, st1/sc1 for throughput or cold data.
Purchasing: premature commitment
Measure usage before committing to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans to avoid wasted cost.
Quick remediation
  • Lock down Security Groups immediately.
  • Run small-scale tests to profile performance.
  • Automate snapshot retention and cleanup.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should retain. First, an EC2 instance is a virtual server offering elastic compute; its flexibility supports scaling and cost control. Second, AMIs are launch templates that capture an instance's OS and software state; use custom AMIs for reproducible deployments. Third, instance types define C P U, memory, storage, and network profiles; choose a family that matches the workload. Fourth, key pairs secure access with a private key you must protect; losing or exposing it requires rotation. Fifth, Security Groups act as stateful firewalls—apply least privilege and avoid opening SSH to the world. Sixth, EBS volumes provide persistent block storage in multiple types; choose gp3, io2, st1, or sc1 based on performance needs. Seventh, snapshots are incremental backups stored externally and must be scheduled and retained according to recovery objectives. Finally, purchasing options—On-Demand, Reserved, Savings Plans, Spot—allow you to balance cost and availability; measure usage before committing. Keep these points in mind as practical rules when designing and operating EC2-based architectures.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what EC2 is, why its elasticity matters, and how the core pieces — AMIs, instance types, key pairs, Security Groups, and EBS — fit together to run production workloads. EC2 gives you virtual servers that start and stop on demand. The elasticity means you can scale compute up or down and pay only for what you use; that capability underlies cost optimization and architectural agility. You will see how an AMI packages an operating system and software so instances launch in a known state, how instance types trade C P U, memory, and storage, and how EBS provides persistent block storage separate from instance lifetime. We will also walk through secure access using key pairs and protect instances with Security Groups. Finally, you will get a hands-on lab walkthrough for launching an Amazon Linux t2. micro instance and installing Nginx. By the end you’ll be able to choose an AMI, pick an appropriately sized instance type, secure it for SSH and HTTP, and attach EBS volumes safely. Think of EC2 as the building block for servers in the cloud and this chapter as the practical toolkit for running them securely and cost-effectively. What workload would you run first on EC2, and why?

Over this chapter you’ll gain four practical competencies that map to architecting and operating EC2 workloads. First, you will explain the core components and benefits of EC2 so you can describe why virtualized, elastic compute matters for scalability and cost control. Second, you’ll identify and differentiate instance types and purchasing options so you can pick the right flavor and pricing model for a workload. Third, you will configure and launch an EC2 instance: select an AMI, choose an instance type, create a key pair, and boot the instance. This is a hands-on skill that bridges architecture to deployment. Fourth, you will implement basic network security using Security Groups and manage EBS volumes for persistent storage, including snapshot strategies for durability. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify that the skill is applied, not just read about. Throughout we emphasize practical decisions: when to use Spot Instances, which EBS volume type suits your database, and how to avoid common security misconfigurations. By the end you’ll be ready to launch a secure web server and reason about trade-offs between performance, durability, and cost in EC2 designs.

This page outlines how you will demonstrate the objectives through practical checks. For describing EC2 components, you will map AMI, instance, key pair, Security Group, and EBS to their roles in a short design sketch. For differentiating instance types and purchasing options, you will pick a family and pricing model for two sample workloads: a steady-state database and a batch analytics job. When launching an instance, you will choose an Amazon Linux AMI, select t2. micro for a low-traffic test server, create a key pair and store the private key securely, and complete a secure SSH connection. For storage and backups, you will attach a gp3 EBS volume and create a snapshot, documenting the snapshot as an incremental backup. Each verification step is about performing the task and reflecting briefly on trade-offs: performance versus cost, availability versus interruption risk. This ensures competency, not just recognition. As you complete each milestone, ask yourself whether the choice minimizes risk and cost for the intended workload. That reflective step is essential before moving to the hands-on launch activity.

An EC2 instance is simply a virtual machine running on AWS infrastructure that provides compute capacity for your application. Think of it as a server you control: you decide the operating system, installed software, and lifecycle. The elastic part of EC2 means instances can be launched or terminated quickly so compute scales with demand; you pay for the capacity you use while it runs. A concrete example is creating an EC2 instance to host a small web application: you select an AMI with the desired operating system, pick an instance type like t2. micro for low traffic, and attach an EBS volume to persist site content. Common misconceptions include assuming an instance automatically backs up data when stopped; EBS volumes remain separate and snapshots are required for backups. Also remember that instance runtime cost stops when you terminate the instance, but attached EBS volumes may still incur charges. The key takeaway is that EC2 gives you precise control over server configuration coupled with the ability to scale and pay only for what you use. When you plan an architecture, ask whether a long-running instance or a more scalable service is the best fit for the workload.

An Amazon Machine Image, or AMI, is the template used to launch an EC2 instance. It contains the operating system and any software you want installed at launch. AWS supplies official AMIs for Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, and Windows Server, and you can create custom AMIs from a configured instance to standardize deployments. A common example is building a custom AMI that includes your application server and dependencies, then launching many instances from that AMI to ensure identical runtime behavior. One pitfall is relying on a public AMI without verifying its contents; create or use vetted AMIs for production. Creating your own AMI helps speed scaling and reduces configuration drift because each launch begins from the same snapshot. Remember that AMIs are region-specific; if you operate across regions, copy AMIs as part of your deployment pipeline. The practical effect is reproducible servers and faster scale-out. Consider AMIs part of your release artifact: they capture a known-good state that can be re-launched reliably when you need more compute. AMIs: Amazon Machine Images means amis package os and software so instances launch consistently; custom amis reduce configuration drift and accelerate scaling.. In practical terms, templates that define an instance's software configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Instance types define the hardware profile for an EC2 instance: C P U, memory, storage capacity, and networking. AWS groups types into families with clear primary uses. General purpose (M series) balances resources for mixed workloads. Compute optimized (C series) favors C P U-heavy tasks like batch compute or high-performance web servers. Memory optimized (R series) suits in-memory databases or analytics, while storage optimized (I series) is for high IOPS disk workloads. Accelerated computing (P/G series) provides GPUs for machine learning or graphics acceleration. A concrete example: choose an R series instance for an in-memory cache or a large in-memory database because it provides high R A M relative to C P U. A common planning error is selecting an instance type based only on C P U numbers without considering memory-to-C P U ratio or network bandwidth; this can cause performance bottlenecks. Right-sizing means profiling your workload and selecting an instance that meets both performance and cost goals. If cost is primary and the workload is fault tolerant, consider a lower-cost family or Spot Instances, but be aware of interruption risk. Matching instance family to workload characteristics is essential for predictable performance and efficient spend.

EC2 purchasing options change the cost and availability trade-offs of your compute. On-Demand lets you pay for capacity by the hour or second with no long-term commitments, ideal for unpredictable or short-lived workloads. Reserved Instances provide significant discounts in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment and suit steady-state workloads where usage is predictable. Savings Plans extend this concept, offering discounts across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda in return for a commitment to a consistent hourly spend, which gives more flexibility than instance-specific reservations. Spot Instances let you use unused capacity at deep discounts for fault-tolerant workloads that can accept interruptions. A concrete scenario: for a nightly batch job that can resume work, Spot Instances may be cost-optimal, while a production database benefits from Reserved pricing for consistency. A common mistake is overcommitting to reservations without measuring steady-state usage, which wastes cost savings if utilization is low. The recommended approach is to measure baseline usage, use Reserved or Savings Plans for the predictable portion, and supplement with On-Demand or Spot for bursts or flexible tasks. That balance achieves cost efficiency without sacrificing required availability.

Key pairs secure SSH access to Linux EC2 instances. A key pair includes a public key, which AWS stores, and a private key file you download and keep locally. When you launch a Linux instance, you assign a key pair so you can SSH into the instance using the private key. Keep the private key file secure; for example, use file permissions that restrict access to your user account. The chapter's hands-on example creates a key pair named my-web-server-key and downloads my-web-server-key. pem. A common mistake is storing the private key in an unsafe location or sharing it. Another misstep is not setting file permissions correctly; SSH clients will refuse to use an insecure key file. For Windows instances, key pairs let you decrypt the administrator password. Practically, treat the private key like a secret credential. If it is lost or compromised, create a new key pair and update access procedures. For automated deployments, use secure secret management and avoid embedding private keys in scripts. Remember: key pairs control direct host access and are a crucial first line of defense for instances.

Security Groups are stateful virtual firewalls that control network traffic to and from EC2 instances. They define allowed inbound and outbound rules by protocol, port range, and source or destination IP ranges. For example, to allow SSH access, add an inbound rule for TCP port 22 from your IP address; to serve a website, allow inbound HTTP on port 80 from anywhere if public access is needed. A frequent security flaw is making rules too permissive, such as allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0, which exposes instances to wide attack surface. Follow the principle of least privilege: open only the ports you need, and restrict the source IP ranges to trusted addresses whenever possible. Security Groups are applied at the instance level, and changes apply immediately to associated instances. Because they are stateful, an allowed inbound connection will automatically allow return traffic; you usually don't need explicit outbound rules for the same connection. Always review Security Group rules during deployment to ensure they match intended access patterns. In practical terms, control inbound and outbound traffic using allowed protocols, ports, and sources. Amazon Elastic Block Store provides persistent block-level storage that you attach to EC2 instances. EBS volumes persist independently from the instance’s lifetime, so your data can survive instance termination when configured to do so. EBS offers multiple volume types for different workload profiles: General Purpose SSD (gp2/gp3) for balanced performance; Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2) for high-performance databases that need predictable IOPS; Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) for large throughput-oriented workloads; and Cold HDD (sc1) for infrequent access. Select a volume type based on IO characteristics and cost. For example, use gp3 for typical application disks and io2 for a production database requiring sustained high IOPS. EBS snapshots create incremental backups stored in object storage, supporting recovery and migration. A typical mistake is using a lower-performance volume for a latency-sensitive workload, which causes degraded throughput. Monitor performance metrics and choose the volume that matches your access pattern. Finally, remember to plan backup and snapshot schedules to meet your recovery objectives. EBS snapshots are incremental backups of EBS volumes stored in object storage, enabling point-in-time recovery and migration. Snapshots save only changed blocks after the initial snapshot, helping to reduce storage costs over time. To ensure durability, schedule regular snapshots based on your recovery point objective and test restores to verify the process. For example, daily snapshots might be appropriate for production databases while weekly snapshots could suffice for less critical data. A frequent oversight is assuming snapshots are instantaneous; depending on volume size and input and output load, snapshots may take time to complete. Another common error is not automating cleanup policies, which can lead to unexpected costs from old snapshots. Implement lifecycle policies that remove or archive snapshots according to retention rules. When restoring, you create a new EBS volume from a snapshot and attach it to an instance. In migration scenarios, snapshots let you copy data across regions by copying the snapshot to the target region and restoring a volume there. Always test your snapshot and restore process to confirm you meet your recovery objectives. This screen highlights common mistakes and how to avoid them when working with EC2. One frequent error is overly permissive Security Groups—allowing SSH from everywhere is risky. Use your specific IP address or a narrow range for SSH. Another mistake is selecting an instance type based only on C P U without considering memory or network bandwidth, which can create bottlenecks. When it comes to storage, choosing a low-cost HDD for a latency-sensitive database will harm performance; select gp3 or io2 according to IOPS and throughput needs. For purchasing options, avoid committing to Reserved Instances before measuring steady-state usage; instead collect usage data and then commit to RIs or Savings Plans for the predictable portion. With key pairs, the common operational issue is losing the private key or storing it in an insecure location; treat it as a secret and rotate when necessary. For snapshots, failing to automate retention leads to uncontrolled costs. The best practices are clear: apply least privilege, right-size based on profiling, automate backups and lifecycle, and test restores. These patterns reduce risk and keep cost predictable.

Let's summarize the essential concepts you should retain. First, an EC2 instance is a virtual server offering elastic compute; its flexibility supports scaling and cost control. Second, AMIs are launch templates that capture an instance's OS and software state; use custom AMIs for reproducible deployments. Third, instance types define C P U, memory, storage, and network profiles; choose a family that matches the workload. Fourth, key pairs secure access with a private key you must protect; losing or exposing it requires rotation. Fifth, Security Groups act as stateful firewalls—apply least privilege and avoid opening SSH to the world. Sixth, EBS volumes provide persistent block storage in multiple types; choose gp3, io2, st1, or sc1 based on performance needs. Seventh, snapshots are incremental backups stored externally and must be scheduled and retained according to recovery objectives. Finally, purchasing options—On-Demand, Reserved, Savings Plans, Spot—allow you to balance cost and availability; measure usage before committing. Keep these points in mind as practical rules when designing and operating EC2-based architectures.

To finish, here are three compact reminders to anchor your practice. First, secure access: never leave SSH wide open; use key pairs and restrictive Security Group rules. Second, match resources: choose instance families and EBS types that align with C P U, memory, IOPS, and throughput needs to avoid performance surprises. Third, protect data and cost: use incremental EBS snapshots with lifecycle policies and choose the purchasing option mix—Reserved or Savings for predictable usage and Spot for interruptible tasks—to keep costs under control. These three checks cover the most common operational decisions you’ll make as a Solutions Architect working with EC2. When in doubt, measure workload behavior, apply least privilege, and automate backups and retention. That approach reduces risk and keeps your deployments reliable and cost-effective.
